"Exceptionable" means open to objection — that is, something people could reasonably object to, criticize, disapprove of, or find inappropriate. If something is exceptionable, it is the kind of thing that deserves complaint or refusal. The word is essentially a more formal way of saying "objectionable."
The key to understanding it: "taking exception"

Think about the phrase "to take exception to something." When you take exception to something, you are objecting to it — you are saying "I have a problem with this." Now, something that is "exceptionable" is literally something you can take exception to. Something worth objecting to. The two ideas are directly connected, and keeping this link in mind will make the word stick.
"Exceptionable" is never a compliment. If you describe something as exceptionable, you are criticizing it. There is no neutral or positive use of this word.
The most important thing: do not confuse it with "exceptional"

This is the single biggest trap with this word, and it trips up even educated speakers. "Exceptionable" and "exceptional" look almost identical, but they mean something entirely different — and they point in nearly opposite emotional directions.

"Exceptional" means extraordinary, unusually impressive, or standing out from the norm — almost always a positive description. "She is an exceptional cook" is a compliment.

"Exceptionable" means objectionable, worthy of criticism or disapproval. "His comments were exceptionable" means his comments were the kind that people would rightly object to.

So one word praises, and the other criticizes. Mixing them up leads to serious misunderstanding.

"His behavior toward the guests was exceptionable." → His behavior was something people could rightly object to or find offensive.

"Nothing in the agreement was exceptionable." → There was nothing in the agreement that anyone could legitimately object to.

"The journalist found the politician's remarks highly exceptionable." → The journalist found the remarks deeply objectionable.

"Her conduct, while unconventional, was not exceptionable." → Even though she did things differently, nobody could reasonably find fault with her conduct.

Notice how in each case, the word points toward something being disputed, criticized, or found inappropriate — or, when used with "not," it clears something of that charge.

"Exceptionable" is a formal, literary word. You will rarely hear it in everyday conversation — people would simply say "objectionable," "unacceptable," "inappropriate," or "offensive" instead. It tends to appear in formal essays, legal contexts, literary criticism, and older writing. Because it is rare and easily confused with "exceptional," using it in casual writing can backfire if your reader doesn't know it well. But in the right formal context, it is a precise and elegant word.

Anchor it to this phrase: to take exception. Taking exception = objecting. Exceptionable = something worth objecting to. If you can remember that link, you will never forget what the word means — and you will never confuse it with "exceptional" again.
